subtype: Minority view that turned out right [Observer]
passage:
Monday. In the launch meeting, Indu said the supplier’s delivery date was unrealistic. Eight of them nodded past her and moved on. Rekha thought Indu was being negative.
Twelve days later the supplier missed the date. The launch slipped, and the team sat in a quiet room. Someone said, “Indu did say.” Nobody answered.
The following Friday the manager thanked Indu in front of everyone. Rekha, at the back, felt an odd distance from herself. She had nodded with the rest. It struck her that being outnumbered had nothing to do with being wrong.

qa.q: What did Indu say in the launch meeting?
qa.a: Indu said the supplier's delivery date was unrealistic.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel at the back of the room when the manager thanked Indu?
qa.a: Rekha felt oddly detached and thoughtful, aware that she had nodded with the rest. The realisation that being outnumbered is not the same as being wrong shows in her reflection.

qa.q: What could the team do differently the next time someone raises a concern?
qa.a: They could ask the person to explain the reasons before moving on and note the concern in the plan. That would treat a lone warning as information.

qa.q: How might Indu have felt when everyone nodded past her, and again when the manager thanked her?
qa.a: Indu was probably frustrated and unheard in the meeting, and later validated but perhaps also uneasy that it took a missed date. The passage shows only what people said.

grounding: Shows an observer recalling a lone voice that warned of a problem the group dismissed, and that being outnumbered does not mean being wrong.

subtype: Minority view that turned out right [Observer]
passage:
Salma, come here. I’m Kashish, and I’ll tell you about a lake picnic when I was twenty-two. Our college group had hired two boats, and someone had tied up the smaller one for the second load.
Meena, a quiet girl from our class, said, “That boat has a crack near the back.” Everyone laughed. “Always worrying,” they said.
Meena did not laugh back. She said again, calmly, “Please, look at it.” I looked, and I wanted to say she was right, but I stayed quiet.
Then the boatman checked, and the boat was not used. It leaked within minutes. Nobody said sorry to Meena, but they never called her a worrier again.

qa.q: How old was Kashish at the lake picnic?
qa.a: Kashish was twenty-two.

qa.q: How might Meena have felt when everyone laughed at her warning?
qa.a: Meena was probably embarrassed and worried, but she stayed calm and repeated it. Not laughing back shows she cared more about safety than the mocking.

qa.q: What choice did Meena make that turned out to matter?
qa.a: Meena repeated calmly, “Please, look at it,” instead of dropping the warning when laughed at. That got the boat checked before anyone used it.

qa.q: How might the boatman have felt about Meena's warning?
qa.a: The boatman probably took it seriously once it was raised, since the boat was checked and withdrawn. The passage shows only that action.

grounding: An elder recalls a lone voice warning of a cracked boat that the group laughed at and that turned out to be right.

passage: Harsha still remembers the night of the college fest, three years ago. It had rained all afternoon, and the fifteen-member organising committee was rushing to open the gates by six. Shreya, a quiet electrical engineering student, said the cables behind the main stage were lying in puddles and should be moved before the power went on. The committee head laughed. 'We don't have time. It's fine.' Most people agreed; the crowd was already queueing. Harsha said nothing. Shreya went, alone, to the college electrician. He came, looked, and cut the power. The fest started an hour late, and people grumbled. Later the electrician showed them a scorched junction box. Harsha thinks of Shreya every time a room agrees too quickly.

qa.q: Where were the cables lying?
qa.a: In puddles behind the main stage.

qa.q: What does Harsha feel when remembering that night?
qa.a: Uneasy and regretful about staying silent, which is why Harsha thinks of Shreya whenever a room agrees too quickly.

qa.q: What did Shreya do that turned out right?
qa.a: She went alone to the college electrician, who cut the power and later found a scorched junction box.

qa.q: How might Shreya have felt when the committee head laughed?
qa.a: Dismissed and alone, but sure enough of the danger to act anyway.

grounding: An observer remembers a lone student whose safety warning the group dismissed, and who turned out to be right.

subtype: Minority view that turned out right [Observer]
passage: Mehak still tells new colleagues at the Mumbai office about Sudha. Two years ago, the whole accounts team wanted to switch to a new billing system over one weekend. At the meeting, Sudha, the most junior person, said, 'We haven't tested it with the old client records. We might lose them.' The manager said she was being negative. The others agreed; everyone was tired of the old system. Mehak remembers thinking Sudha was probably just nervous. They switched. On Monday morning, three years of client records had vanished. It took two weeks to rebuild them from paper files. Sudha never said 'I told you so'. She just helped rebuild. Since then, Mehak has made a habit of asking the quietest person in a meeting what they think.

qa.q: How long did it take to rebuild the records?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: What does Mehak feel when remembering Sudha's warning?
qa.a: Mehak feels regretful and humbled, having assumed Sudha was just nervous.

qa.q: What habit has Mehak taken from this?
qa.a: Asking the quietest person in a meeting what they think, because a lone warning can be right.

qa.q: How might Sudha have felt when the records vanished?
qa.a: Probably frustrated and sad, but she chose to help rebuild instead of saying 'I told you so'.

grounding: An observer remembers a junior colleague's dismissed warning that proved right, and learns that being outnumbered is not being wrong.

subtype: Minority view that turned out right [Observer]
passage:
'Remember the society meeting about the basement parking?' Gautam asked, stirring his tea.
Jyoti groaned. 'Don't.'
'You were the only one who said the drain was too small. Sixty families voted against you.'
'Mr Arora called me a pessimist.'
'And then the first monsoon came.'
'Forty cars under water.' Jyoti laughed, but not happily. 'I didn't want to be right.'
'I voted with them, you know. I thought sixty people can't be wrong.'
'They could. They were just tired, and the smaller drain was cheaper.'
Gautam looked out at the new drain the society had finally built. 'Now, whenever everyone agrees fast, I think of you standing up alone with that drain map.'
'Next time,' Jyoti said, 'stand up with me.'

qa.q: How many cars went under water?
qa.a: Forty cars.

qa.q: How does Gautam feel remembering his vote?
qa.a: Gautam feels regretful, having assumed sixty people couldn't be wrong.

qa.q: What lesson does Gautam take from this?
qa.a: That being outnumbered doesn't mean being wrong, so when everyone agrees fast he should look again and stand with the lone voice.

qa.q: What did Jyoti mean by 'I didn't want to be right'?
qa.a: Jyoti felt no satisfaction, only sadness, since being right meant forty families' cars were flooded.

grounding: An observer recalls a lone neighbour's dismissed warning about a drain that proved right, and what it taught him.

subtype: Minority view that turned out right [Observer]
passage: I'm Suraj. At my first job, a small app start-up in Kochi, there was a quiet tester called Zubin. Two weeks before our big launch, he stood up in the morning meeting and said the payment page crashed on older phones. He had tested it on his cousin's handset. The founder laughed. "Who uses a phone that old?" Everyone else nodded, me included. We had a launch party to plan. Zubin said it once more, calmly, then sent an email with screenshots. Nobody replied. On launch day the support inbox filled up by noon: half our users were in small towns, on exactly those phones. We spent a week fixing it. The founder never mentioned the email. I did. I went to Zubin's desk and said, "You were right, and I nodded along." Now, whenever a room agrees too fast, I think of him.

qa.q: What did Zubin say crashed on older phones?
qa.a: The payment page.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling on going to Zubin's desk?
qa.a: Suraj felt regretful and a little ashamed for having nodded along, and wanted Zubin to know he had been right.

qa.q: What could the team have done differently when Zubin warned them?
qa.a: They could have checked Zubin's screenshots before dismissing him, since being outnumbered did not make him wrong.

qa.q: What might Zubin have felt when nobody replied to the email?
qa.a: He probably felt ignored and frustrated, yet stayed calm and put the evidence in writing.

grounding: Suraj remembers a lone tester whose warning the group dismissed and who turned out to be right.
